title: The Truth About All-Inclusive in Šibenik 2027
metaDescription: Does Šibenik have all-inclusive hotels? Yes, in Solaris resort. What is included, rough € prices vs half-board and apartments, and who should self-cater.
content:
## Myth 1: Šibenik has no all-inclusive hotels

The city itself has almost none, but the Solaris resort on the coast does. Amadria Park Hotel Ivan, in the Solaris complex roughly 4–6 km from the old town, is offered as all-inclusive by package operators. The Amadria Park hotels around it (Jure, Niko, Jakov and the Kids Hotel Andrija) are mostly sold with breakfast, half-board or room-only rates. Those rates vary by operator. D-Resort Šibenik, by the marina, is sold with breakfast, and Armerun Heritage Hotel in the old town is listed with all-inclusive options on some platforms. Check the board type on the booking page before you pay, because it changes by date and operator.

**Better alternative:** book the Ivan package through an operator, or pick half-board at one of the Amadria hotels and keep the old town for lunches.

## Myth 2: All-inclusive here means unlimited everything

This is a Dalmatian version. Expect breakfast, lunch and dinner buffets, snacks at set times, and house wine, beer, soft drinks and water at meals or from the bars. Premium spirits, spa treatments, sports extras, towels for the beach and excursions to Krka are normally charged separately. Parking costs about €12 a day, and a tourist tax of around €2 per adult per night applies from April to September.

On Tripadvisor, one guest at Hotel Punta in nearby Vodice complained that a package sold as all-inclusive was really full board, with drinks only at meals. The point holds: read what is included before you book.

**Better alternative:** ask the hotel in writing which drinks and hours are covered.

## Myth 3: All-inclusive is the cheap way to do Croatia

It is not. Room rates at Hotel Ivan run roughly €110–€170 per night for a double in the shoulder months, and more in July and August. Rough per-person nightly figures for two adults sharing:

| Option | Peak (July–August) | Shoulder (May–June, September) |
|---|---|---|
| All-inclusive, Solaris hotel | €110–€180 | €65–€100 |
| Half-board, same area | €90–€140 | €55–€85 |
| Private apartment, self-catering | €30–€60 for the apartment share, plus €25–€40 for food | €20–€40, plus €25–€35 for food |

Apartments at the Solaris resort itself list from about €65 per night in low season up to about €245–€315 in peak depending on size, so even resort apartments undercut a hotel. These are estimates, not quotes. Operator package prices fluctuate widely.

One opinionated point: paying all-inclusive rates for a week at Solaris while planning Krka and Primošten day trips is a waste. You will pay for lunches you skip, and the main sights are 16–25 km away.

**Better alternative:** half-board, so dinner is covered and lunch is flexible.

## Myth 4: All-inclusive is right for every family

It works for families with children under about 10 on stays of 3–7 nights. The hotel has pools and an aquapark nearby, kids' programmes and a beach front, so nobody needs a car or restaurant bookings. Cribs cost about €7 per day.

It works poorly for stays beyond a week, groups with teenagers who want the town, and anyone driving to Krka, Skradin or the islands daily.

**Better alternative:** self-catering with a kitchen in an apartment in Šibenik old town or at Solaris. A supermarket shop for four runs about €25–€40 a day, and a konoba dinner is still cheaper than the board supplement.

## Myth 5: If Šibenik is short on all-inclusive, go elsewhere

Nearby options exist, but you rarely need them. Vodice, about 12 km north, has Matilde Beach Resort and Hotel Punta, both listed with all-inclusive and board options. They are more of a beach-resort setting, with a livelier summer waterfront than Solaris. Choose them for a longer beach stay, but Solaris is the closest to the old town.

## Which Stay Fits Which Šibenik Traveller

- **Families with small children, 3–7 nights:** all-inclusive at the Solaris resort in shoulder season, when prices drop and the pools are quieter.
- **Couples and sightseers:** half-board at most, or an old town apartment.
- **Groups, long stays, budget travellers:** self-catering wins by a wide margin.

Insider note: shoulder-season dates in late May, June and September can cut the package price by a third or more, with the sea warm enough for children.

faq.question: But isn't there only one all-inclusive hotel in Šibenik?
faq.answer: The clearest all-inclusive offer is Amadria Park Hotel Ivan at the Solaris resort. Armerun Heritage Hotel in the old town is also listed with an all-inclusive option on some platforms. Availability depends on the operator and dates, so confirm the board type before booking.

faq.question: Isn't all-inclusive always cheaper than paying for meals separately?
faq.answer: Not here. Rough estimates are €110–€180 per person per night in peak season, against €90–€140 for half-board. Restaurant meals in Šibenik are moderate, so guests who eat out at lunch usually spend less with half-board or an apartment.

faq.question: Doesn't all-inclusive include drinks all day?
faq.answer: Usually not around the clock. Typical Croatian packages cover meals, snacks and selected house drinks at set hours. Premium drinks, spa, parking (about €12 a day) and excursions are normally extra.

faq.question: Is all-inclusive good for toddlers and young children?
faq.answer: Yes, for short stays. Buffets, pools and a beach on site remove daily decisions, and cribs cost about €7 per day. For stays of 10 days or more, a kitchen apartment is cheaper and gives more flexibility.

faq.question: Where is the nearest all-inclusive if Solaris is full?
faq.answer: Vodice, around 12 km north, has Matilde Beach Resort and Hotel Punta, both sold with board options. Confirm what each package covers before booking.

faq.question: How does a private apartment compare on price?
faq.answer: Much cheaper. Resort apartments at Solaris start around €65 per night in low season, and old town apartments are often lower. Adding about €25–€40 per person for groceries and some meals still usually costs less than all-inclusive.

quickAnswer: Most people assume Šibenik has no all-inclusive at all, or that it works like Turkey or Egypt. Neither is true. The Solaris resort, about 6 km from the old town, sells all-inclusive packages, mainly through tour operators. Expect a lighter, pricier version than the Mediterranean standard. It suits families with small children on short stays.
